document.title: USSR: Withdrawal from Afghanistan (SNIE 11/37/88, Key Judgments only)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: Excerpts from a March 1988 SNIE giving an American assessment of a "firm" Soviet decision, based on a "leadership consensus," to withdraw from Afghanistan. Originally published in CIA, At Cold War's End (1999).

persons.name: Mikhail Gorbachev
persons.role: General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party; built leadership consensus for withdrawal from Afghanistan

mentions.quote: we believe General Secretary Gorbachev has built a leadership consensus for withdrawal.
ending the war will be a net plus for Gorbachev, boosting his popularity and his reform agenda.

persons.name: Najibullah
persons.role: Head of the Kabul Communist regime

mentions.quote: We judge that the Najibullah regime will not long survive the completion of Soviet withdrawal

organizations.name: Soviet Politburo
organizations.notes: Consensus for withdrawal could fracture in an alternative scenario.

organizations.name: Kabul regime
organizations.notes: Soviet client regime; assessed unlikely to survive long after Soviet withdrawal.

organizations.name: Afghan resistance
organizations.notes: Assessed to retain supplies and strength despite infighting; coalition of traditionalist and fundamentalist groups expected.

organizations.name: National Foreign Intelligence Board
organizations.notes: Concurred in and approved the Estimate on 24 March 1988.

organizations.name: Geneva accords
organizations.notes: Negotiations under whose cover the Soviets wanted to withdraw.

events.description: Estimate approved by the National Foreign Intelligence Board; information cutoff date.
Soviets expected to begin withdrawal from Afghanistan this year even if the Geneva talks are deadlocked.
National Foreign Intelligence Board approved SNIE 11/37-88 on Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan; information available as of this date was used.
Assessed Soviet start of troop withdrawal from Afghanistan this year, even if the Geneva talks are deadlocked.
Estimate judges that the Soviet leadership made a firm decision to withdraw from Afghanistan.
Geneva talks on accords governing withdrawal were ongoing and possibly deadlocked.

key_claims: Moscow has made a firm decision to withdraw from Afghanistan.
Soviets would likely begin withdrawal in 1988 even if the Geneva talks deadlock, probably with heavy fighting.
The Najibullah regime will not long survive Soviet withdrawal and may fall before it is complete.
The resistance will retain sufficient supplies and strength to topple the Communist government despite infighting.
The successor regime is expected to be an unstable fundamentalist/traditionalist coalition, Islamic but not as extreme as Iran, with ambivalent or hostile orientation toward the West.
There is under a one-in-three chance of prolonged chaos from resistance infighting.
Withdrawal is expected to complicate US relations with Pakistan.
